question: Which statement best describes The base case?
options: Every recursive function needs at least one base case: a condition simple enough to answer directly without recursing further. The base case is what stops the recursion — without it, the function calls itself forever and the program crashes. Always write the base case first so you can reason about when the calls end.

These two are the classic teaching examples. Factorial multiplies a number by the factorial of one less (n * factorial(n-1)), with base case 1. Fibonacci adds the two previous numbers (fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)), with two base cases. Fibonacci also shows recursion's danger: the naive version recomputes the same values exponentially, which memoization fixes.

Each function call is pushed onto the call stack with its own local variables and its own place to return to. A recursive function stacks up one frame per call until it hits the base case, then those frames unwind (pop off) one by one as each call returns its value to the one beneath it. Understanding this push/unwind flow is the heart of reading recursion.

The recursive case is the part that calls the function again on a smaller or simpler input, moving steadily toward the base case. The key discipline is that each call must reduce the problem — otherwise it never reaches the base case. You combine the result of the smaller call with a little local work to build the full answer.

Any recursion can be rewritten as a loop and vice versa. Recursion is often clearer for problems with a naturally nested or branching structure (trees, JSON, divide-and-conquer), while loops are usually faster and use constant memory because they don't grow the call stack. Choose recursion for readability on nested data and iteration for performance-critical linear work.

Recursion shines on data that contains more of itself: the DOM, file systems, nested comment threads, or deeply nested JSON. You handle one node, then recurse into each child. The recursive shape mirrors the data's shape, which is why it reads so naturally compared to manual stacks or queues.

A tail call is when the recursive call is the very last thing a function does, so no extra work happens after it returns. The ES2015 spec describes tail-call optimization that would reuse the stack frame, but in practice almost no JavaScript engines implement it (Safari is the notable exception). Treat tail recursion as a nice idea, not a safety net — for deep recursion, prefer iteration.
